secretAnswer: A puzzle jug is a drinking vessel with holes and hidden passages that make it hard to drink without spilling.
supportingFacts: Its neck has holes, so simply tipping it does not work.
It was used for drinking games in taverns.
revealExplanation: The V&A's recreated jug has a hidden route under the handle. Covering all but one spout lets the drinker use suction.

sources.title: V&A — How was it made? A puzzle jug

secretAnswer: A fuddling cup joins several drinking cups inside, so emptying one can draw liquid from all of them.
supportingFacts: The cups look separate but their inner spaces are connected.
Such cups were used as joke drinking pots in English taverns.
revealExplanation: A drinker who expects one small cup can end up drinking the contents of the whole group.

sources.title: Seattle Art Museum — Object of the Week: Triplicate vase

secretAnswer: A vinaigrette box is a small container for a sponge soaked in scented vinegar.
supportingFacts: A lid with small holes holds the sponge while letting its smell out.
People could wear it at the waist or neck, or carry it in a pocket.
revealExplanation: Silver examples had gold-covered interiors to protect the silver from the vinegar.

sources.title: The Met — William Thompson II, Vinaigrette

secretAnswer: A netsuke is a small toggle that helps hold a hanging container on a Japanese kimono's waist sash.
supportingFacts: A cord links the toggle to the container.
Wood and ivory were common materials, and many examples are tiny carved figures.
revealExplanation: These useful objects also let their owners show wealth through fine materials and skilled carving.

sources.title: The Met — Netsuke: From Fashion Fobs to Coveted Collectibles

secretAnswer: An aquamanile is a vessel used to pour water over someone's hands for washing.
supportingFacts: Medieval examples could be shaped like animals or a mounted knight.
They were used by priests and by people at the dining table.
revealExplanation: On the Met's knight-shaped example, the helmet opens for filling, and water comes out near the horse's head.

sources.title: The Met — Aquamanile in the Form of a Mounted Knight

secretAnswer: A chatelaine is a waist hook with chains that carry small useful objects.
supportingFacts: Its chains could hold keys, scissors, a watch or a small purse.
It attaches to a belt, sash or waistband.
revealExplanation: It could also show the authority of the person who kept the keys of a large household.

sources.title: ASU FIDM Museum — Chatelaine purse

secretAnswer: A miser's purse is a long coin purse with a small middle opening that sliding rings close.
supportingFacts: Coins can be kept in either end of the purse.
Many examples were knitted or crocheted, often with beads.
revealExplanation: Some had differently shaped ends so the owner could find the right coins by touch in poor light.

sources.title: National Museum, Bloemfontein — The Miser's purse

secretAnswer: A porte-bouquet is a small decorative holder for a bunch of fresh flowers.
supportingFacts: It is also called a posy holder.
Holders were made from materials such as silver, gold and mother-of-pearl.
revealExplanation: They could be gifts for important occasions; Queen Victoria received a rich example during a visit to France.

sources.title: The Fan Museum — Come to the Ball: Posy Holders and Pretty Fans

secretAnswer: The Burghley Nef is a rich salt container made in the shape of a ship.
supportingFacts: Its hull is a nautilus shell with silver mounts partly covered in gold.
It was made in Paris in the sixteenth century.
revealExplanation: Ship-shaped table objects like this could mark the place of a host or honoured guest and show their status.

sources.title: V&A on Google Arts & Culture — The Burghley Nef

secretAnswer: An epergne is a table centrepiece used to display fruit, sweets or flowers.
supportingFacts: The Met has an example made from bronze covered in gold.
That example belonged to a set with matching candle holders.
revealExplanation: The Met's example was owned by Elizabeth Schuyler, Alexander Hamilton's widow.

sources.title: The Met — Richmond Room, Epergne

secretAnswer: A noken is a knotted or woven bag made by communities in Papua, Indonesia.
supportingFacts: It is made by hand from wood fibre or leaves.
People use it to carry things such as food, firewood and even babies.
revealExplanation: A noken can also be worn at traditional celebrations or given as a peace offering.

sources.title: UNESCO — Noken multifunctional knotted or woven bag

secretAnswer: Silbo Gomero is a way of communicating Spanish words through whistles on the island of La Gomera.
supportingFacts: Different whistle sounds stand for vowels and consonants.
Pitch and breaks in the whistles help listeners tell the sounds apart.
revealExplanation: It is passed from skilled users to learners and has also been taught in schools.

sources.title: UNESCO — Whistled language of La Gomera, the Silbo Gomero

secretAnswer: Yimakan is Hezhen storytelling that mixes spoken stories and singing without musical instruments.
supportingFacts: Performers use different melodies for different characters and parts of a story.
Stories include heroes, battles and the defeat of monsters.
revealExplanation: The practice also carries community history and customs, and learners often train with an experienced storyteller.

sources.title: UNESCO — Decision 20.COM 7.c.2, Hezhen Yimakan storytelling

secretAnswer: Momoeria is a New Year celebration with dance, acting and music in villages in northern Greece.
supportingFacts: Performers move through village streets and visit homes.
The celebration runs from Christmas Day into early January.
revealExplanation: Its dancers wear helmets, pleated skirts and traditional shoes, and carry sticks.

sources.title: UNESCO — Decision 11.COM 10.b.16, Momoeria

secretAnswer: Al-Qatt Al-Asiri is a tradition of painting geometric patterns on interior walls in Asir, Saudi Arabia.
supportingFacts: Guest rooms are a special focus for this decoration.
The patterns are usually made on a white gypsum base.
revealExplanation: Women have traditionally taught the skill by inviting female relatives to help decorate their homes.

sources.title: UNESCO — Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, interior wall decoration in Asir

secretAnswer: Aitysh is a contest where two performers invent spoken or sung poems in response to each other.
supportingFacts: The performers sit opposite each other and respond to topics chosen by the audience.
They accompany their verses with traditional string instruments.
revealExplanation: This tradition in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan values humour, quick thinking and thoughtful ideas.

sources.title: UNESCO — Aitysh/Aitys, art of improvisation

secretAnswer: Táncház is a Hungarian way of learning folk dance and music through active group practice.
supportingFacts: Learners watch and copy experienced dancers while live music plays.
People can take part regardless of age or previous dance experience.
revealExplanation: The name means dance house. Singing lessons and craft activities can also accompany the dancing.

sources.title: UNESCO — Táncház method: a Hungarian model

secretAnswer: A bourdaloue is an oval portable chamber pot designed for a woman to use.
supportingFacts: Examples could be made from decorated porcelain.
The Holburne Museum's example was made at the Meissen factory.
revealExplanation: One museum example was altered after damage and may later have been mistaken for a plant pot.

sources.title: The Holburne Museum — Meissen Porcelain Bourdaloue

secretAnswer: A stay busk is a stiff piece placed at the front of a corset to help it keep its shape.
supportingFacts: The Met has a curved wooden example.
Busks could be decorated with rare wood or mother-of-pearl.
revealExplanation: Makers sometimes put great effort into decorating this piece even though it was usually hidden by clothing.

sources.title: The Met — Busk
London Museum — Busk, stay busk, scrimshaw

secretAnswer: A niddy-noddy is a tool for winding yarn into loose bundles called hanks or skeins.
supportingFacts: Yarn is wound in a figure of eight around crosspieces at its ends.
The Highland museum's example is made of wood.
revealExplanation: It helped prepare spun wool for knitting. The museum's old example has darkened after years in peat smoke.

sources.title: Museum of the Highlands — Crios-iarna or Niddy-noddy

secretAnswer: A lucet is a small fork-shaped tool used to make braided cord from thread.
supportingFacts: A typical lucet has two prongs at one end.
Its cord is strong, slightly springy and square in shape.
revealExplanation: The basic technique uses one continuous thread; the cord can serve as clothing laces or bag ties.

sources.title: Hyland House Museum — Build a Lucet Tool and Braid Cords

secretAnswer: A pounce pot holds powder that is sprinkled on paper to help prepare it for writing or dry ink.
supportingFacts: Small holes in its top let the powder fall through.
A shallow dish on top can catch extra powder.
revealExplanation: Pounce could be made from materials such as pumice, tree resin or ground cuttlefish bone.

sources.title: The Village at Black Creek — Pounce Pot

secretAnswer: A spill vase stores thin wood strips or rolled paper used to carry a flame to a candle or lamp.
supportingFacts: These strips or rolls are called spills.
They offered a cheap way to light things when matches were expensive.
revealExplanation: The Brunel Museum's example has a flat back so it can stand neatly against a wall on a mantelpiece.

sources.title: Brunel Museum — Why doesn't this vase have room for flowers?

secretAnswer: A clog almanac is a wooden calendar marked with days and symbols for important dates.
supportingFacts: Its symbols can mark saints' feast days.
It can also mark important dates in the farming year.
revealExplanation: The British Museum holds a Norwegian example with marks for days and weeks.

sources.title: British Museum — Clog-almanac, 1928,0313.1

secretAnswer: A hornbook is a small handled board that carries a protected sheet for children learning letters and numbers.
supportingFacts: A thin clear layer of horn, or sometimes mica, protects the printed sheet.
Many sheets also include the Lord's Prayer.
revealExplanation: The small board could hang from a child's belt so its lessons stayed close at hand.

sources.title: Library of Congress — A Child's Introduction to the Alphabet

secretAnswer: Syllabub is a sweet English treat made by mixing wine with cream or milk to form a light froth.
supportingFacts: Historical recipes could add sugar and lemon.
Some versions have creamy foam above a layer of wine.
revealExplanation: An everlasting syllabub used more cream and less wine, making a thicker dessert.

sources.title: US National Library of Medicine — Sup on a Syllabub

secretAnswer: A hidden fore-edge painting is a picture on a book's page edges that appears when the pages are fanned out.
supportingFacts: The artist paints the pages while they are fanned and held in a clamp.
Gold is applied to the closed edges to hide the picture.
revealExplanation: Some books have two hidden pictures, with a different scene revealed when the pages are fanned the other way.

sources.title: University of Sydney Library — Hidden Fore-edge Paintings

secretAnswer: A misericord is a small ledge under a folding church seat that supports a person when the seat is raised.
supportingFacts: It is part of a hinged seat in the choir stalls.
Its underside can carry carved scenes, sometimes with comic or rude subjects.
revealExplanation: The Art Fund's Bristol example is carved in oak and shows a joke involving an archer.

sources.title: Art Fund — Misericord, Bristol Museum & Art Gallery

secretAnswer: Frumenty is a thick dish of wheat cooked in milk or broth.
supportingFacts: Some versions are sweetened and flavoured with cinnamon.
Its name comes from the Latin word for grain.
revealExplanation: A medieval recipe book includes a version served with porpoise, showing how different old menus could be.

sources.title: Weston Museum — Recipes Through Time: Frumenty
London Museum — A Sainsbury's history of Christmas pudding

secretAnswer: A mazer is a wooden drinking bowl, often made from maple and fitted with a metal rim.
supportingFacts: Surviving examples have rims made of silver or silver covered in gold.
Some have words or decorative designs on them.
revealExplanation: One bowl in the Met advises its drinker to think a lot and speak less.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press — On the English medieval drinking bowls called Mazers
The Met — Drinking Bowl, 55.25
